slides: So, there are two templates we recommend for the opening paragraph. Each one has its own advantages. Let's go through them.
The first one is the minimal template.
You rewrite the background, describe the dispute very briefly, add a sentence saying there are people against it, and then your position. That's it.
The second one: rewriting the whole task text.
The background, the positions, the arguments, everything that's there, just a bit shorter. And your position at the end.
Okay, the minimal template. Here it is, with the slots you fill in.
First slot: what's happening. Who is doing what, or proposing what.
Second slot: what it's for. And notice something. While I'm rewriting the background, I'm actually presenting side A. Because the purpose of the plan is side A's argument.
And then just one sentence: however, some oppose this move. And my position.
I don't go into arguments. I don't say the supporters say this, and the opponents say that. Minimal.
Now, there are a few ways to phrase that last sentence. Pick one, and make it yours.
So, four options. Whether you're against or for, you can always fit your position into the last part of the sentence.
And careful with the English here. It's 'I agree'. Never 'I am agree'.
Let's see an example with our running task. Face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
The first part is just the background, rewritten. And while I'm rewriting it, I'm presenting side A: it's meant to help catch offenders.
Then I add one sentence: however, some people oppose this move. And my position: I agree with them.
Minimal, short, a good paragraph. If the rest of your essay is excellent, the whole essay is excellent. This paragraph does the job perfectly.
And its advantage? It's short and quick. I don't have to think too much. Rewrite the background, 'however, some oppose', position, go.
Now the second template: rewriting the task text.
I said the task text is kind of a perfect opening. Maybe a bit long, but perfect. So, let's rewrite it.
Everything in the task text goes in. Some task texts only give arguments for one side, so then I rewrite one side. If they give both sides, I rewrite both.
The advantage is... I don't need to decide what's background and what's an argument. No risk. I just go on automatic: every sentence there, I rewrite it and make it a bit shorter.
Here are some phrase options for each slot.
Now, 'the former' means the first group you mentioned, and 'the latter' means the second. Precise, and short.
And for a complex position: I take this side, provided that... or, although we'd need some safeguard.
Let's see the rewrite version for the cameras.
Notice, 'as long as their images are stored in a database' wasn't in the minimal version. And neither was 'before or during an offence, or afterwards'.
Here I don't decide what's important. Everything in the task text goes in, just worded a little differently.
So who are 'the former'? The supporters. And look, I'm already showing a complex position. I choose this side, but I get that I need some reservations, to protect the other side's concern too.
So one advantage of the rewrite template is... no thinking. The task text goes in, all of it.
Another advantage: it makes the essay richer. The paragraph comes out much longer than the minimal one. And not because of padding or repeating things. All of it is relevant.
So who does it help? Students whose essays are too short, who barely get to twenty-five lines. And, as we'll see, anyone who drops an argument paragraph.
There's also a small psychological thing here. Raters know a well-developed essay tends to be longer. And a very short one makes them wonder if the arguments were really developed.
Just remember, extra length only helps when it's relevant content. Writing more and drifting off topic isn't better. Good essays are usually about thirty to forty lines.
Now, the downside.
Not every student can rewrite well. Some try, get stuck, and spend ages on it.
So if rewriting is hard for you, leave it. Work with the minimal template.
Otherwise you'll be stuck on the horse's tail for a very, very long time... and you won't finish the rest of the essay.
Okay, that's it for the opening. Now we go to the other end, the part that closes the essay: the closing paragraph.
Now it's your turn. Workshop fourteen, opening paragraphs. It's in the card right after this lesson.
Do it before you move on. Each assignment builds on the one before, and by the end of the lessons, you'll have written whole essays.
